newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Rebels dig in as Albania army advances.
newsitem.headline: Rebels dig in as Albania army advances.

text.p: Armed rebels remained in control of towns in the Albanian south on Thursday as army and police forces closed in to try to stifle the insurrection shaking the Balkan state. President Sali Berisha was quoted as assuring the Italian government, however, that his forces would not seek to retake the rebel-held towns by force. Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told reporters that Berisha had given assurances that the army would seek to isolate the towns and then try to reach a settlement for the rebels to lay down their arms. Soldiers had fought with insurgents east of the Adriatic port of Sarande on Wednesday in the first serious clash reporters have witnessed since Albania's parliament declared a state of emergency in response to spreading rioting and anarchy.

Army and police, clearly in control of the town of Fier, 120 km (75 miles) south of Tirana, guarded checkpoints on roads leading to the port of Vlore, where at least 20 people have been killed since the rebellion erupted last Friday.

Armed groups, apparently lacking any command structure, threw up roadblocks on a road near Tepelene, more than 90 km (55 miles) southeast of Fier in Albania's rugged interior, reporters who travelled to the area said.

In Tepelene itself, a Reuter reporter saw anti-government groups, mainly youths, in firm control, rolling big-calibre guns into the central square. The Interior Ministry said two people were killed in Vlore on Wednesday night following clashes between armed bands driving cars in the streets in the town.
A government information official said army and police forces were progressing towards Vlore but were moving slowly to avoid increasing tension.
"There have been no deaths caused by the military or police and no person from the armed forces has been killed," the official said.
A reporter in the town of Gjirokaster, where trouble also broke out at the weekend, said the government was in control.
A Western diplomatic source said there had been no substantial change in Vlore where barricades had been erected amid a breakdown of law and order.
Armed gangs in Delvine, about 15 km (10 miles) east of Sarande, had seized tanks and destroyed a bridge on the road to Gjirokaster with the aim of keeping government forces out, the source said.

In Tirana, members of political parties from the right and left, including the ruling Democrats and main opposition Socialists, were seen by reporters entering the presidency building on Thursday morning.
But it was not immediately clear whether they were to meet President Berisha, who has been urged by foreign governments to seek a settlement with the opposition to end political instability.
Parliament, dominated by the Democratic Party which re-elected Berisha to a second five-year term as president on Monday, had also been convened.
Berisha removed the government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi on Saturday following weeks of protests sparked by the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes.
But opposition parties, demoralised since the state of emergency measures were introduced, seek the establishment of a government of technocrats before early elections.
The president has offered to hold early polls but has refused to enter any coalition with the Socialists, reformed heirs of the former Stalinist regime that ruled Albania for 45 years until 1990.
